To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the germination of seeds and the growth of seedlings of plants colonizing loose volcanic matter are not inhibited by the presence of the other species, 2) the species composition of the pioneer vegetation is determined by the seed bank and the seed dispersal of species, and 3) the seed bank is formed by the seeds of species that are not able to germinate in loose volcanic matter.
the plants of the studied species are able to colonize loose volcanic matter and to form monodominant stands of pioneer species on loose volcanic material.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: What are the specific features of plants at the early stages of colonization of loose volcanic material?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the plants growing on loose volcanic matter are characterized by the following: (1) a high rate of growth, especially in height and leaf surface area; (2) a short life cycle, with the majority of species flowering and setting seed within a year; (3) an abundance of seeds, with the majority being small, and a large number of seeds produced per individual; (4) a high germination rate, and (5) an ability to germinate in the absence of light.
the species studied are characterized by high adaptability and plasticity of the vegetative and generative organs, which is a necessary prerequisite for their survival on the volcanic substrata.

the species composition of the pioneer plant community depends on the type of loose volcanic matter (volcanic ash, tephra, pumice, etc.), the degree of its consolidation and the age of the volcanic matter.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
plants of the first stage of colonization of volcanic matter are characterized by a low degree of specialization and a high degree of plasticity.
in loose volcanic material, plants with small seeds and seedlings are better adapted to the conditions than those with large seeds and seedlings.
the species studied are characterized by high seed germination and seedling survival rates and by high seedling growth rates.
The main takeaway from our work is that
plants growing on loose volcanic matter have specific features that allow them to survive in the harsh environment of volcanic islands.
the colonization of loose matter by plants is a complex and multi-stage process.

the plants growing in the loose volcanic matter are not only able to germinate in the conditions of the substrate, but also to survive the first stages of the colonization process, which is characterized by a high degree of instability.
